title: Design a URL shortener
prompt: Design a service that turns long URLs into short links and redirects visitors to the original page. Users can optionally pick a custom alias and set an expiry.
assumptions: 100M new links per month
Reads outnumber writes 100 to 1
Redirects should feel instant (p99 under 100 ms)
Links are retained for 5 years

clarifications.question: What features must the service support?
clarifications.answer: Create a short link from a long URL, redirect from the short link, optional custom alias, optional expiry date. Link deletion by the owner is included.

clarifications.question: How many links and how much traffic?
clarifications.answer: 100M new links per month, so about 6B links over 5 years. Redirect traffic is 100x writes, roughly 4k redirects/s on average and about 12k/s at peak.

clarifications.question: What latency do redirects need?
clarifications.answer: p99 under 100 ms measured at the service, p50 under 20 ms. Creation can take up to 300 ms.

clarifications.question: How available must it be?
clarifications.answer: Redirects target 99.99%. Creation can degrade briefly to 99.9%.

clarifications.question: Any constraints on the short code?
clarifications.answer: Codes use [a-zA-Z0-9], 7 characters by default. Codes must not be guessable in sequence, and custom aliases are 4-20 characters.

clarifications.question: If the same long URL is submitted twice, do we return the same code?
clarifications.answer: No. Each submission gets a new code, which keeps per-link analytics and expiry independent.

clarifications.question: Do we need click analytics?
clarifications.answer: Only basic click counts and referrer, computed asynchronously. Counts may lag by a few minutes. Detailed dashboards are out of scope.

clarifications.question: Should redirects be 301 or 302?
clarifications.answer: Use 302 so every click reaches us for analytics and expiry checks. Mention the trade-off if you prefer 301.

clarifications.question: What can we skip?
clarifications.answer: User accounts UI, billing, malware scanning, and multi-region active-active writes.

title: Design a chat app like WhatsApp
prompt: Design a chat application that supports one-to-one and group messaging with delivery receipts, offline delivery and media sharing.
assumptions: 500M daily active users
Each user sends about 40 messages per day
Online messages are delivered within 500 ms
Groups hold up to 256 members

clarifications.question: What must the app support?
clarifications.answer: 1:1 chat, group chat up to 256 members, sent/delivered/read receipts, online presence, offline message delivery, and image/video sharing.

clarifications.question: How large is the user base and traffic?
clarifications.answer: 500M DAU at 40 messages each is 20B messages/day, about 230k messages/s on average and roughly 500k/s at peak. Assume about 200M concurrent connections.

clarifications.question: What delivery latency do we target?
clarifications.answer: p99 under 500 ms for an online recipient in the same region, under 1 s cross-region.

clarifications.question: Do messages need ordering?
clarifications.answer: Yes, per conversation. Global ordering is not needed. Messages must never be lost once the sender gets the server ack.

clarifications.question: How long do we keep undelivered messages?
clarifications.answer: 30 days. Once delivered to all of a user's devices the server deletes its copy. Chat history lives on the device.

clarifications.question: Is the chat end-to-end encrypted?
clarifications.answer: Yes. The server stores and routes ciphertext only, so no server-side search. Key exchange details are out of scope.

clarifications.question: How are photos and videos handled?
clarifications.answer: Clients upload to object storage and send a message containing the media URL and key. Media up to 100 MB, kept 30 days if undelivered.

clarifications.question: Multi-device support?
clarifications.answer: Out of scope for the first version. One active device per account.

clarifications.question: How accurate is last-seen and online status?
clarifications.answer: Best effort. A few seconds of staleness is fine, and it must not generate a write per heartbeat.

title: Design a rate limiter
prompt: Design a rate limiter that restricts how many requests a client can make to an API in a given time window across a fleet of servers.
assumptions: 1M requests per second across the fleet at peak
10M distinct clients (API keys or IPs)
Typical rule: 100 requests per minute per client
Limiter adds under 5 ms to a request

clarifications.question: Where does the limiter run?
clarifications.answer: As middleware in the API gateway layer, in front of all backend services. A shared library for service-to-service calls is a stretch goal.

clarifications.question: What do we limit by?
clarifications.answer: API key or user id when authenticated, otherwise IP address. Rules can also be per endpoint.

clarifications.question: Are limits configurable?
clarifications.answer: Yes. Rules like 100/min per user and 10/s per endpoint live in a config store and reload within 30 seconds without a deploy.

clarifications.question: How strict must counting be?
clarifications.answer: Approximate is fine: within 5-10% of the limit. Never allow wildly more than the limit, and do not block valid traffic.

clarifications.question: What does a limited client see?
clarifications.answer: HTTP 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.

clarifications.question: If the limiter store is down, what happens?
clarifications.answer: Fail open for general APIs so we do not cause an outage. Sensitive endpoints such as login can fail closed.

clarifications.question: Is it multi-region?
clarifications.answer: Limits are enforced per region with an optional slow global sync. Exact global limits are out of scope.

clarifications.question: Do we allow bursts?
clarifications.answer: Yes, short bursts up to 2x the per-second rate are acceptable, which suggests a token bucket.

Fail open vs fail closed
Strict global limit vs regional enforcement

title: Design a news feed
prompt: Design a news feed where users see a ranked list of recent posts from people they follow.
assumptions: 300M daily active users
Each user opens the feed about 5 times a day
50M new posts per day
Average user follows 500 accounts, celebrities have up to 50M followers

clarifications.question: What does the feed show?
clarifications.answer: Posts from followed accounts: text plus image or video links. Users can create posts, follow people, and scroll the feed with pagination. Likes and comments are out of scope.

clarifications.question: What are the read and write rates?
clarifications.answer: 1.5B feed reads/day is about 17k/s average and 50k/s peak. 50M posts/day is about 580 posts/s.

clarifications.question: How fast should the feed load?
clarifications.answer: p99 under 500 ms for the first page of 20 posts.

clarifications.question: How fresh must the feed be?
clarifications.answer: A new post should appear in followers' feeds within 5 seconds for normal users and within about 30 seconds for celebrities.

clarifications.question: Is the feed chronological?
clarifications.answer: Start with reverse chronological, then discuss a ranking stage that scores candidates using recency, affinity and engagement.

clarifications.question: What does the follower distribution look like?
clarifications.answer: Average 200 followers per author, but a long tail: roughly 0.1% of authors have over 1M followers and the top few have 50M.

clarifications.question: What consistency does a user expect?
clarifications.answer: A user must see their own post immediately. Other users can see eventually consistent feeds.

clarifications.question: How much feed history do we keep?
clarifications.answer: Feeds precompute the latest 500 posts per user. Older items are fetched from the post store on demand.

title: Design a notification service
prompt: Design a notification service that sends push, SMS and email messages to users on behalf of many internal product teams.
assumptions: 1B notifications per day across all channels
Peak traffic is about 5x average
Marketing blasts can target 50M users within 10 minutes
Time-critical messages such as OTP must arrive within 5 seconds

clarifications.question: Which channels do we support?
clarifications.answer: Mobile push (APNs and FCM), SMS and email through third-party providers. In-app inbox is optional.

clarifications.question: What volume do we expect?
clarifications.answer: 1B/day is about 11.5k/s average and about 58k/s peak. A 50M blast in 10 minutes needs about 83k/s sustained.

clarifications.question: Are all notifications equal?
clarifications.answer: No. OTP and security alerts are high priority with a 5 second target. Transactional messages target 30 seconds. Marketing is best effort over minutes.

clarifications.question: Do users control what they receive?
clarifications.answer: Yes. Per-channel and per-category opt-out, quiet hours, and a global unsubscribe that must always be honored.

clarifications.question: What delivery semantics do we promise?
clarifications.answer: At least once to the provider, with deduplication so users do not see duplicates. Final delivery depends on provider and device.

clarifications.question: Do callers send raw text?
clarifications.answer: Callers send a template id plus parameters. The service renders by user locale.

clarifications.question: Any limits per user?
clarifications.answer: Max 5 marketing notifications per user per day. Transactional is not limited.

clarifications.question: Do we track outcomes?
clarifications.answer: Yes: sent, delivered, opened, failed. Statuses are exposed through an API and events, with minutes of lag acceptable.

title: Design a video streaming platform
prompt: Design a video streaming platform where creators upload videos and viewers stream them on phones, browsers and TVs.
assumptions: 200M daily active viewers watching about 1 hour each
500k new videos uploaded per day, 10 minutes long on average
Playback should start within 2 seconds
Peak concurrency is about 10% of daily users

clarifications.question: What features are in scope?
clarifications.answer: Upload, transcoding, adaptive-bitrate playback, search by title, and view counts. Live streaming, recommendations and comments are out of scope.

clarifications.question: How many viewers stream at once?
clarifications.answer: 200M DAU, about 20M concurrent at peak. At an average 3 Mbps that is about 60 Tbps of egress, which must come from CDNs.

clarifications.question: How large are uploads and how fast must they be available?
clarifications.answer: Source files average 1.5 GB, up to 20 GB. Videos should be playable at lower quality within 5 minutes and fully transcoded within 30 minutes.

clarifications.question: What formats and resolutions?
clarifications.answer: A ladder from 240p to 4K in H.264 and a subset in VP9/AV1, packaged as HLS and DASH with 4-6 second segments.

clarifications.question: How much storage per video?
clarifications.answer: About 1 GB across all renditions per video, so about 500 TB/day of new storage. Cold videos move to cheaper tiers.

clarifications.question: What are the availability expectations?
clarifications.answer: Playback 99.99%. Upload and processing can tolerate 99.9%.

clarifications.question: Can view counts be approximate?
clarifications.answer: Yes. Counts can lag by minutes and use approximate aggregation. Video metadata is eventually consistent but a creator sees their own change immediately.

clarifications.question: Do we handle copyright or moderation?
clarifications.answer: Mention a hook for it in the pipeline but do not design the classifier.

title: Design a ride-hailing service
prompt: Design a ride-hailing service that matches riders with nearby drivers, tracks the trip and computes the fare.
assumptions: 10M rides per day
1M drivers online at peak, each sending location every 4 seconds
A rider should be matched within 5 seconds
Ride requests peak at about 5x the daily average

clarifications.question: What flows must we support?
clarifications.answer: Rider requests a ride, system finds and offers it to nearby drivers, live tracking during the trip, ETA and fare estimate. Payments and ratings are out of scope.

clarifications.question: What are the traffic numbers?
clarifications.answer: 10M rides/day is about 115 requests/s average and 600/s at peak. 1M drivers x 1 update per 4 s is 250k location updates/s.

clarifications.question: How is a driver chosen?
clarifications.answer: Nearest available drivers by ETA within a radius, offered to one driver at a time with a 10 second accept window, falling back to the next.

clarifications.question: What latency targets apply?
clarifications.answer: Match within 5 seconds at p95. Rider sees driver location updates every 4 seconds with under 1 second delivery lag.

clarifications.question: Can a driver be matched to two riders?
clarifications.answer: No. Driver assignment must be strongly consistent for a single driver. Location data can be eventually consistent.

clarifications.question: How long do we keep location history?
clarifications.answer: Live positions are kept in memory only. Trip routes are persisted for 90 days for disputes and fare checks.

clarifications.question: How large is the service area?
clarifications.answer: Hundreds of cities worldwide, partitioned by region. Cross-city matching is not needed.

clarifications.question: Is surge pricing required?
clarifications.answer: Mention it as a per-area multiplier computed from the demand/supply ratio. Full pricing design is out of scope.

title: Design a file storage and sync service
prompt: Design a file storage and sync service where users keep files in the cloud and see changes synced across their devices.
assumptions: 50M users with about 2 GB stored on average
10M daily active users
Files up to 10 GB, split into 4 MB chunks
Changes should sync to other devices within 10 seconds

clarifications.question: What does the service do?
clarifications.answer: Upload and download files, automatic sync across multiple devices, file and folder sharing, version history. Real-time collaborative editing is out of scope.

clarifications.question: How much data and activity?
clarifications.answer: 50M users x 2 GB is 100 PB. With 10M DAU doing about 20 sync operations each, metadata ops are about 200M/day or 2.3k/s average.

clarifications.question: How are large files handled?
clarifications.answer: Files are split into 4 MB chunks, each identified by a content hash. Only changed chunks are uploaded, and identical chunks are deduplicated.

clarifications.question: How fast must changes propagate?
clarifications.answer: Other online devices learn of a change within 10 seconds via a notification, then pull the diff.

clarifications.question: What consistency do users need?
clarifications.answer: Metadata is strongly consistent per user. Concurrent edits to the same file create a conflicted copy rather than silently overwriting.

clarifications.question: What durability is required?
clarifications.answer: Eleven nines for file data, achieved with replication or erasure coding across zones. Metadata is replicated synchronously.

clarifications.question: How much history do we keep?
clarifications.answer: 30 days of versions for free users and 1 year for paid. Deleted files stay in trash for 30 days.

clarifications.question: What about encryption?
clarifications.answer: Encrypt in transit and at rest. Client-side end-to-end encryption is out of scope.

title: Design search autocomplete

assumptions: 500M searches per day
Suggestions requested on about 5 keystrokes per search
Suggestions must appear within 100 ms
Top 10 suggestions per prefix

clarifications.question: What exactly do we return?
clarifications.answer: Up to 10 completions for the typed prefix, ranked by popularity. Personalization and spell correction are stretch goals.

clarifications.question: How many requests?
clarifications.answer: 500M searches x 5 = 2.5B suggestion requests/day, about 29k/s average and 100k/s at peak.

clarifications.question: What is the latency target?
clarifications.answer: p99 under 100 ms end to end, so the server work should be under 20 ms.

clarifications.question: How fresh must suggestions be?
clarifications.answer: Trending queries should appear within 15 to 30 minutes. A full rebuild runs daily.

clarifications.question: How many distinct queries?
clarifications.answer: About 100M distinct queries of 25 characters average, roughly 2.5 GB raw text, fitting in memory when compressed.

clarifications.question: How do we rank?
clarifications.answer: By recent query frequency with time decay. Offensive or blocked terms are filtered.

title: Design a web crawler
prompt: Design a web crawler that discovers and downloads pages from the internet for a search engine to index.
assumptions: 1B pages crawled per month
Average page is 100 KB
Pages are recrawled based on how often they change
The crawler must be polite to every site

clarifications.question: What is the crawler responsible for?
clarifications.answer: Fetch pages, extract links, store content for the indexer, and schedule recrawls. Indexing and ranking are out of scope.

clarifications.question: What throughput is required?
clarifications.answer: 1B pages/month is about 385 pages/s on average. Provision for 1,000 pages/s to catch up after outages.

clarifications.question: How much do we store?
clarifications.answer: 1B x 100 KB is 100 TB/month raw, about 30 TB compressed. We keep the latest copy per URL plus a short history.

clarifications.question: How often are pages recrawled?
clarifications.answer: Adaptive: news sites hourly, typical pages every 1-4 weeks, static pages monthly or less, estimated from observed change rates.

clarifications.question: What rules must we follow?
clarifications.answer: Obey robots.txt, limit to about 1 request per second per host, and honor crawl-delay and per-host back-off on errors.

clarifications.question: Which content types?
clarifications.answer: HTML only at first. Images, PDFs and JavaScript-rendered pages are extensions.

clarifications.question: How do we handle duplicates?
clarifications.answer: Deduplicate URLs after normalization and detect near-duplicate content via hashing such as simhash.

clarifications.question: Do we worry about crawler traps?
clarifications.answer: Yes. Limit URL depth, URL length, and pages per host, and detect infinite calendar-like URL patterns.

title: Design a distributed cache
prompt: Design a distributed in-memory cache that application services use to reduce load on their databases.
assumptions: 1M operations per second
5 TB of cached data, average value 1 KB
90% reads and 10% writes
p99 latency under 5 ms

clarifications.question: What operations does the cache offer?
clarifications.answer: GET, SET with TTL, DELETE, and atomic increment. Rich data structures and pub/sub are out of scope.

clarifications.question: How much traffic and data?
clarifications.answer: 1M ops/s total (900k reads, 100k writes) over about 5 TB of data.

clarifications.question: What latency is required?
clarifications.answer: p99 under 5 ms from clients in the same region, p50 under 1 ms.

clarifications.question: How consistent must the cache be?
clarifications.answer: Eventual. A single key has a single primary, so reads from the primary are consistent. Stale reads from replicas for a short period are acceptable.

clarifications.question: What happens when a node fails?
clarifications.answer: The cache must remain available. Losing data is acceptable because the database is the source of truth, but we want to avoid a stampede on the database.

clarifications.question: How do we evict?
clarifications.answer: LRU-style eviction when memory is full, plus TTL expiration. The policy is configurable per cache namespace.

clarifications.question: Who is the client?
clarifications.answer: Internal services through a smart client library that knows the cluster topology.

clarifications.question: Do we expect skewed keys?
clarifications.answer: Yes. A handful of keys can receive 100k reads/s, and the design must handle them.

Replication factor 3

clarifications.question: How big is the system?
clarifications.answer: 100 TB of logical data x 3 replicas is 300 TB physical. Traffic is 500k ops/s with a 70/30 read/write mix.

clarifications.question: What is more important, availability or consistency?

clarifications.question: What consistency model is expected?
clarifications.answer: Tunable per request: quorum for strong-ish behavior (R + W > N) or single replica for speed. Eventual consistency with conflict resolution is the default.

clarifications.question: What are the latency targets?
clarifications.answer: p99 under 10 ms for reads and writes within a region.

clarifications.question: How do we avoid losing writes?
clarifications.answer: A write is acknowledged after reaching W replicas and the commit log. Data survives loss of any two nodes.

clarifications.question: Is it multi-region?
clarifications.answer: Single region first, with cross-region async replication as a stretch goal.

clarifications.question: How are conflicting writes resolved?

title: Design a ticket booking system
prompt: Design a ticket booking system for events where thousands of users compete for a limited number of seats and no seat may be sold twice.

Seats are held for 10 minutes during checkout

clarifications.question: What flows are included?
clarifications.answer: Browse events, view the seat map, select seats, hold them while paying, and confirm the booking. Resale and refunds are out of scope.

clarifications.question: What is the peak load?
clarifications.answer: 500k users arrive within minutes of sale start. Seat map reads reach 100k/s. If the event sells out in 5 minutes, that is about 170 bookings/s with maybe 10x as many hold attempts.

clarifications.question: Can we ever double-sell a seat?
clarifications.answer: Never. Seat state transitions must be atomic. Overselling is worse than turning users away.

clarifications.question: How do holds work?
clarifications.answer: Selecting a seat creates a hold for 10 minutes. If payment is not completed, the hold expires and the seat returns to the pool automatically.

clarifications.question: How do we handle the stampede?
clarifications.answer: A virtual waiting room admits users in batches (e.g. 5k at a time) so downstream services stay within capacity.

clarifications.question: How is payment handled?
clarifications.answer: Via an external payment provider. Our flow must be idempotent and handle payment success after a hold has expired.

clarifications.question: What can be eventually consistent?
clarifications.answer: The seat map shown to browsers can lag a couple of seconds. The booking decision itself is strongly consistent.

clarifications.question: What if the system is overloaded?
clarifications.answer: Degrade gracefully by queueing and shedding load at the edge rather than failing checkout.

title: Design a payment system
prompt: Design a payment system that lets merchants accept card payments through external payment service providers and keeps accurate financial records.
assumptions: 10M payments per day
Peak around 1,000 payments per second
Money must never be lost or double charged
Financial records retained for 7 years

clarifications.question: What does the system do?
clarifications.answer: Create a payment for an order, authorize and capture via a PSP, handle refunds, and expose payment status. We do not store raw card numbers; the PSP tokenizes.

clarifications.question: What volume?
clarifications.answer: 10M/day is about 115/s average and about 1,000/s at peak (sales events).

clarifications.question: What is the key correctness requirement?
clarifications.answer: Exactly-once effect: a retry or timeout must never charge a customer twice. Every payment ends in a known final state.

clarifications.question: How long can a payment take?
clarifications.answer: Authorization within 2-3 seconds at p95, dominated by the PSP. Our overhead should be under 200 ms.

clarifications.question: How is money tracked internally?
clarifications.answer: A double-entry ledger where each payment creates balanced debit and credit entries. The ledger is append-only.

clarifications.question: Do we reconcile with PSPs?
clarifications.answer: Yes, daily. PSP settlement files are compared against our ledger, and mismatches create alerts and manual review tasks.

clarifications.question: What if a PSP times out?
clarifications.answer: The payment is marked pending. We query status or wait for a webhook. We never assume failure and retry the charge blindly.

clarifications.question: Any compliance needs?
clarifications.answer: PCI DSS: do not store card data, encrypt sensitive fields, audit access. Detailed fraud detection is out of scope.

prompt: Design a metrics and monitoring system that collects metrics from servers, stores them, and supports dashboards and alerting.
assumptions: 100k hosts each emitting 100 metrics every 10 seconds
Alerts should fire within 1 minute of a problem
Keep full-resolution data for 15 days and downsampled for 13 months
Dashboard queries return in under 1 second

clarifications.question: What features are needed?
clarifications.answer: Metric ingestion, time series storage, query for dashboards, and alerting with notifications. Logs and traces are out of scope.

clarifications.question: What is the ingest rate?
clarifications.answer: 100k hosts x 100 metrics is 10M active series. At one point per 10 s that is 1M data points/s.

clarifications.question: How much storage?
clarifications.answer: A raw point is about 16 bytes, but time-series compression reaches about 2 bytes. 1M x 86,400 x 2 B is about 170 GB/day compressed; 15 days is about 2.6 TB before replication.

clarifications.question: What query latency?
clarifications.answer: p99 under 1 s for dashboard queries over the last 24 hours. Longer ranges hit downsampled data.

clarifications.question: How do alerts work?
clarifications.answer: Rules evaluated every 30-60 seconds over recent data, with thresholds and duration conditions. Notifications go to on-call tools. Alerts must not be lost.

clarifications.question: Push or pull?
clarifications.answer: Either is acceptable. Discuss both; assume agents on each host that push to collectors.

clarifications.question: Can users add labels freely?
clarifications.answer: Labels are allowed but high-cardinality labels (user IDs) are rejected or limited, since they explode series count.

clarifications.question: How available must it be?
clarifications.answer: Ingest and alerting 99.99%. Dashboards can degrade. The monitoring system must not depend on the systems it monitors.

prompt: Design a distributed message queue where producers publish messages to topics and consumers read them reliably.
assumptions: 500k messages per second sustained, 1M at peak

Replication factor 3

clarifications.question: What does the queue provide?
clarifications.answer: Topics with partitions, publish, consume via consumer groups, and acknowledgements. Stream processing and schema registry are out of scope.

clarifications.question: What are the throughput numbers?
clarifications.answer: 500k msgs/s x 1 KB is 500 MB/s sustained and 1 GB/s at peak, across thousands of topics.

clarifications.question: How long is data kept?
clarifications.answer: 3 days by default, configurable per topic. Consumers can replay from any retained offset.

clarifications.question: What delivery semantics?
clarifications.answer: At-least-once by default. Exactly-once is a stretch goal using idempotent producers and transactions.

clarifications.question: What ordering do we guarantee?
clarifications.answer: Strict ordering within a partition. No ordering across partitions. Producers pick the partition via a key.

clarifications.question: What latency is expected?
clarifications.answer: End-to-end p99 under 20 ms at normal load, with acknowledged writes durable on a quorum.

clarifications.question: How durable are acked messages?
clarifications.answer: With acks=all, a message survives the loss of any two replicas. It is replicated to in-sync replicas before ack.

clarifications.question: How do consumers scale?
clarifications.answer: Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group, so parallelism equals partition count. Group rebalancing handles membership changes.

50k rank lookups per second

clarifications.question: What does the leaderboard support?
clarifications.answer: Submit or increment a score, get the top N players, get a player's rank and score, and view the players ranked around them. Seasonal resets are included.

clarifications.question: What is the load?
clarifications.answer: 50M players, about 20k score updates/s on average and 100k/s at peak, plus 50k rank queries/s.

clarifications.question: How real-time must it be?
clarifications.answer: Top-100 and own rank must be accurate within 1 second.

clarifications.question: How are ties handled?
clarifications.answer: Tie-break by earliest time the score was achieved.

clarifications.question: How often does the board reset?
clarifications.answer: Monthly seasons. Old seasons are archived and read-only.

clarifications.question: Global only?
